dx: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and nail pitting
case: A 41-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of pain and swelling in several fingers and toes. He also has a 2-year history of low back pain. He has had scaly plaques on his elbows and scalp since his 20s. Physical examination shows diffuse swelling of the entire left third finger and right second toe, tenderness of the distal interphalangeal joints of both hands, and pitting and onycholysis of several fingernails. Chest expansion is 2.0 cm (expected for his age, about 5 cm or more). Serum rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are negative. HLA-B27 testing is positive. MRI shows bilateral sacroiliitis. Diagnosis: psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis, nail disease, and axial involvement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the diffuse swelling of his left third finger?
options: Synovitis confined to the metacarpophalangeal joint
Tenosynovitis and enthesitis along the whole digit
Lymphatic obstruction from chronic skin inflammation
Periosteal new bone from hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
approach: Note the clue: the whole finger and a whole toe are swollen, not just one joint.
Recall that a sausage digit (dactylitis) reflects inflammation of the flexor tendon sheath, the entheses, and the soft tissue along the digit.
Contrast this with rheumatoid arthritis, where inflammation stays inside the synovium of individual joints.
questions.why: Dactylitis is a hallmark of psoriatic arthritis and other spondyloarthritides. Imaging shows flexor tenosynovitis, enthesitis, soft tissue edema, and synovitis of several joints in the same digit, so the whole finger swells like a sausage. Rheumatoid arthritis instead causes symmetric synovitis of MCP and PIP joints with sparing of the DIP joints. DIP involvement, dactylitis, nail pitting, negative RF and anti-CCP, and pencil-in-cup erosions all point to psoriatic arthritis.
whyNot: Synovitis limited to a joint gives fusiform swelling around that joint only. Joint-centered synovitis of the MCP and PIP joints is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, which spares the DIP joints.
Correct.
Lymphedema from skin disease is not a recognized cause of a sausage digit. The swelling here comes from inflamed tendon sheaths and entheses beneath the skin.
Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy causes clubbing and periostitis of long bones, usually with lung disease. It does not produce a single tender, swollen digit.

questions.stem: Before the skin and nail findings were recognized, reactive arthritis was considered because he had fever and bloody diarrhea 4 weeks before his joint symptoms began. A stool culture from that illness that grew which of the following organisms would have most supported reactive arthritis?
options: Vibrio cholerae
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Bacillus cereus
Shigella flexneri
approach: Identify the illness: fever with bloody diarrhea means an invasive enteric pathogen.
Recall the triggers of reactive arthritis: Chlamydia trachomatis and invasive enteric bacteria (Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter).
Pick the invasive organism from the list; the others act through toxins without invading.
questions.why: Reactive arthritis is a sterile arthritis that begins 1 to 4 weeks after a genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or an enteric infection with Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, or Campylobacter. These organisms invade the mucosa, and bacterial antigens reach the joints. In HLA-B27 positive people the immune response to these antigens drives arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis, and keratoderma blennorrhagicum. Joint cultures are negative.
whyNot: Vibrio cholerae causes profuse watery diarrhea through cholera toxin without invading the mucosa. It is not a classic trigger of reactive arthritis.
Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes watery traveler's diarrhea through heat-labile and heat-stable toxins. It does not invade the mucosa and is not a classic trigger.
Bacillus cereus causes a short food poisoning from preformed or locally made toxins. It is not linked to reactive arthritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of his low back pain is most likely?
options: Prolonged morning stiffness that eases with exercise
Pain that worsens with activity and is relieved by rest
Pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise
Leg pain on walking downhill that is relieved by sitting forward
approach: Link the findings: HLA-B27, sacroiliitis on MRI, and reduced chest expansion mean axial spondyloarthritis like ankylosing spondylitis.
Recall that this back pain is inflammatory, from enthesitis and sacroiliitis.
Inflammatory back pain stiffens with rest and loosens with movement, the opposite of mechanical pain.
questions.why: Axial disease in psoriatic arthritis behaves like ankylosing spondylitis. Inflammation at the sacroiliac joints and the entheses of the spine makes the back stiff after rest, so stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes in the morning and wakes patients in the second half of the night. Movement and exercise improve it, while rest makes it worse. Over years, syndesmophytes can bridge the vertebrae and produce a bamboo spine.
whyNot: Correct.
Pain that worsens with use and improves with rest is mechanical back pain, as in muscle strain or degenerative disc and facet disease.
Radiation below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise points to a herniated disc compressing a lumbar or sacral nerve root.
Leg pain on walking that eases with forward flexion is neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis, usually in older adults.

questions.stem: Pulmonary function testing is performed because of his reduced chest expansion. Which of the following patterns is most likely?
options: Low FEV1/FVC ratio with a high total lung capacity
Normal spirometry with an isolated low DLCO
Low FVC with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Low FEV1/FVC ratio with a high residual volume
approach: Identify the cause of low chest expansion: inflammation and fusion of the costovertebral and costotransverse joints.
A rigid chest wall limits how far the lungs can expand, which is extrapulmonary restriction.
Restriction lowers FVC and FEV1 together, so the FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal or rises.
questions.why: Spondyloarthritis that involves the thoracic spine can fuse the joints where the ribs meet the vertebrae. The rib cage then moves little, so lung volumes fall even though the airways and alveoli are normal. Spirometry shows a low FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio. Other extra-articular complications of ankylosing spondylitis include anterior uveitis, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, and fractures of the fused spine after minor trauma.
whyNot: A low ratio with a high total lung capacity is obstruction with hyperinflation, as in emphysema. A stiff chest wall cannot hyperinflate.
An isolated low DLCO with normal spirometry suggests pulmonary vascular disease or early interstitial disease. Chest wall restriction does not impair gas transfer.
Correct.
A low ratio with air trapping is the pattern of obstructive disease such as asthma or COPD, not a fused rib cage.

dx: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) of the knee in hemochromatosis
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of a painful, swollen right knee. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, darkening of his skin, and erectile dysfunction. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). The right knee is warm and has a large effusion. Radiographs show linear calcification of the menisci and articular cartilage, and hook-like osteophytes at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. Serum ferritin is 2,400 ng/mL (24 to 336), and transferrin saturation is 78% (20 to 50). Genetic testing shows homozygosity for the C282Y mutation in HFE. Synovial fluid has 18,000 leukocytes/mm3, calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and a negative Gram stain. Diagnosis: acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) secondary to hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.stem: Under compensated polarized light microscopy, the crystals in his synovial fluid are most likely to have which of the following appearances?
options: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent
Flat plates with notched corners
Small nonbirefringent clumps staining with alizarin red
Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent
approach: Name the crystal from the case: calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate.
Recall its shape and optical sign: rhomboid or rod-shaped, weakly positive (blue when parallel to the slow axis).
Contrast urate crystals, which are needles with strong negative birefringence (yellow when parallel).
questions.why: Pseudogout is acute arthritis from calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals shed from calcified cartilage. The crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped and weakly positively birefringent. Radiographs often show chondrocalcinosis, and the knee and wrist are the usual joints. In a patient under about 60, chondrocalcinosis should prompt a search for hemochromatosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia. Gout, by contrast, favors the first MTP joint and shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent urate crystals.
whyNot: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals are monosodium urate, the crystal of gout.
Flat plates with notched corners are cholesterol crystals, seen in chronic effusions such as long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals are too small to be birefringent and are identified with alizarin red. They cause calcific tendinitis and Milwaukee shoulder.
Correct.

questions.stem: Arthroscopy of the knee 3 months later shows a partial-thickness defect in the femoral articular cartilage that does not reach the subchondral bone. Which of the following best describes the expected healing of this defect?
options: Little repair, because no vessels deliver repair cells
Complete regeneration of hyaline cartilage within weeks
Filling with fibrocartilage from marrow-derived cells
Replacement by woven bone that later remodels
approach: Note that the defect does not reach the vascular subchondral bone.
Recall that articular cartilage has no blood vessels, nerves, or lymphatics and is fed by diffusion from synovial fluid.
Without vessels, no inflammatory or repair cells reach the defect, so it persists.
questions.why: Articular cartilage is avascular. Healing in most tissues depends on blood vessels that bring inflammatory cells, fibroblasts, and stem cells, so a defect confined to cartilage shows almost no repair. If a defect goes through to the subchondral bone, marrow cells enter and fill it with fibrocartilage, which is mostly type I collagen and wears less well than hyaline cartilage. Tendons heal slowly for a similar reason: they have a sparse blood supply and few cells.
whyNot: Correct.
Adult chondrocytes are locked in lacunae, divide little, and cannot migrate into a defect, so hyaline cartilage does not regenerate.
Fibrocartilage fill happens only when a defect reaches the subchondral bone, so marrow blood and stem cells can enter. This defect stays within the cartilage.
Woven bone forms in fracture callus from vascular tissue. A defect confined to avascular cartilage has no source of bone-forming cells.

questions.stem: Because calcium pyrophosphate deposition can also signal other metabolic disorders, serum studies are ordered. Which of the following sets of results would indicate primary hyperparathyroidism as an additional cause?
options: Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
approach: Start with PTH actions: it raises calcium (bone resorption, renal reabsorption, calcitriol) and lowers phosphate (less proximal tubule reabsorption).
In primary disease the gland makes PTH autonomously, so calcium is high while PTH stays high.
Match the set: high calcium, low phosphate, inappropriately high PTH.
questions.why: In primary hyperparathyroidism, an adenoma secretes PTH that is not suppressed by a high calcium. PTH increases bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption and stimulates calcitriol, so serum calcium rises. PTH also reduces phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so phosphate falls. Alkaline phosphatase may rise with high bone turnover. Hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, and hypomagnesemia are the classic metabolic causes of calcium pyrophosphate deposition.
whyNot: Low calcium with high phosphate and high PTH is secondary hyperparathyroidism, as in chronic kidney disease (renal osteodystrophy).
All-normal values are expected in osteoporosis and would not suggest a parathyroid disorder.
Correct.
High calcium and phosphate with suppressed PTH points to a PTH-independent cause such as vitamin D intoxication.

topics: Serum patterns in metabolic bone disease

questions.stem: His 49-year-old brother has recurrent attacks of severe pain and swelling at the base of the great toe that begin during the night. Which of the following best explains why this distal joint is most often affected in his brother's condition?
options: Higher blood flow delivers more urate to the joint
Lower joint temperature reduces urate solubility
Thicker cartilage adsorbs more urate from plasma
Higher synovial pH promotes urate crystal formation
approach: Recognize nocturnal podagra as acute gout from monosodium urate crystals.
Recall that urate solubility depends on temperature and pH and falls as either drops.
The first MTP joint is cooler than core joints, so urate precipitates there first.
questions.why: Urate is close to its solubility limit in plasma at about 6.8 mg/dL at 37 °C (98.6 °F). Distal joints such as the first MTP joint are several degrees cooler, so urate crystallizes there at lower concentrations. Minor trauma, nighttime fall in temperature, and shifts of water out of the joint add to the risk. Attacks are triggered by alcohol, purine-rich meals, and sudden changes in urate. The fluid shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals, and chronic disease brings tophi and punched-out erosions.
whyNot: The toes are distal and relatively poorly perfused. Blood flow does not explain the predilection, and higher flow would warm the joint.
Correct.
The first MTP joint does not have unusually thick cartilage, and cartilage does not concentrate urate from plasma.
Urate is less soluble at a lower pH, not a higher one. Acidosis favors crystal formation.

dx: De Quervain tenosynovitis in a new mother
case: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician 8 weeks after giving birth because of a 3-week history of pain at the radial side of her right wrist. The pain is worse when she lifts her infant, which she does many times a day with repetitive thumb and wrist motion. She has no history of trauma. Physical examination shows swelling and tenderness over the radial styloid process and pain with resisted extension and abduction of the thumb. Sensation in the hand is normal. Radiographs of the wrist show no abnormalities. Diagnosis: de Quervain tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist.

questions.stem: Which of the following maneuvers is most likely to reproduce her pain?
options: Sustained full flexion of both wrists for 60 seconds
Resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended
Ulnar wrist deviation with the thumb held in a fist
Tapping over the transverse carpal ligament
approach: Name the tendons in the first dorsal compartment: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.
A maneuver that stretches these tendons through their thickened sheath will reproduce pain.
Flexing the thumb into the palm and deviating the wrist ulnarly stretches both tendons over the radial styloid (Finkelstein test).
questions.why: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis as they pass through the first dorsal compartment over the radial styloid. Repetitive thumb abduction and wrist motion, as in lifting an infant, thickens the sheath and narrows the tunnel. The Finkelstein test stretches both tendons by placing the thumb in the fist and deviating the wrist toward the ulna, which reproduces sharp radial wrist pain. Related overuse conditions include plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendinopathy, whose rupture risk rises with fluoroquinolones.
whyNot: Holding the wrists fully flexed is the Phalen test, which reproduces numbness in the median nerve territory in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Pain at the lateral elbow with resisted wrist extension tests lateral epicondylitis at the origin of extensor carpi radialis brevis.
Correct.
Tapping over the carpal tunnel (Tinel sign) produces tingling in median nerve distribution in carpal tunnel syndrome.

topics: Provocative tests of the wrist and elbow

questions.stem: Her pain does not improve with splinting and rest, and surgical release is performed. The excised tendon and sheath show degenerative change with few inflammatory cells. Which of the following changes in the collagen of this tissue is most likely?
options: Thick, parallel type I fibrils with extra cross-links
More type III collagen in thin, disorganized fibrils
Replacement of type I collagen by elastin fibers
Underhydroxylated collagen that cannot form triple helices
approach: Note the clue: degeneration with few inflammatory cells, which is tendinosis.
Recall that repeated microtears are repaired with weaker, immature matrix.
Immature repair matrix has more type III collagen in thin fibrils that lose their parallel alignment.
questions.why: Overuse tendinopathy is mainly a degenerative process (tendinosis) with little inflammation. Repeated loading causes microtears that are repaired with disorganized matrix: a higher share of type III collagen in thin fibrils, increased ground substance, and new small vessels. Type III collagen forms weaker fibrils than the type I collagen of normal tendon, so the tendon is less able to resist tension. The same process causes lateral epicondylitis and supraspinatus tendinopathy.
whyNot: Thick, parallel, well cross-linked type I fibrils are the normal structure that gives tendon its tensile strength. Tendinopathy disrupts this order.
Correct.
Tendinopathy does not convert the matrix to elastin. Elastin is prominent in arteries, lung, and elastic ligaments.
Underhydroxylated collagen is the defect of vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), a systemic disorder unrelated to local overuse.

questions.stem: Her pain also increases when she moves her hand toward the ulnar side at the radiocarpal joint. Which of the following best classifies this joint?
options: Saddle diarthrosis
Pivot diarthrosis
Ball-and-socket diarthrosis
Condyloid diarthrosis
approach: Recall that the radiocarpal joint is a freely movable synovial joint (diarthrosis).
List its movements: flexion, extension, radial deviation, and ulnar deviation, but no axial rotation.
An oval convex surface (scaphoid and lunate) in an oval concavity (distal radius) moving in two axes is a condyloid joint.
questions.why: The radiocarpal joint is a synovial joint, so functionally it is a diarthrosis. The oval convex surface of the proximal carpal row fits into the oval concavity of the distal radius and articular disc. This lets the wrist flex, extend, and deviate toward the radius or ulna, without rotation around its long axis, which defines a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint. Forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints instead.
whyNot: A saddle joint has two surfaces that are each concave in one direction and convex in the other. The first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the example.
A pivot joint allows rotation around one axis, as at the atlantoaxial joint and the proximal radioulnar joint.
A ball-and-socket joint moves around three axes, including rotation, as at the shoulder and hip. The wrist cannot rotate on its own axis.
Correct.

questions.stem: At the visit she mentions that her 66-year-old father has a painless cord in his right palm. His ring finger is held flexed at the metacarpophalangeal joint and cannot be straightened passively, while his flexor tendons glide normally. Which of the following best explains the force that bends his finger?
options: Myofibroblasts contracting within palmar fascia cords
Tonic flexor muscle contraction driven by spinal reflexes
Fibrous ankylosis of the joint after synovitis
Scarring and shortening of the flexor tendon sheath
approach: Locate the problem: a palpable palmar cord with normal tendon gliding means the palmar fascia, not the tendons or joint.
Recall that Dupuytren contracture is a proliferation of myofibroblasts in the palmar fascia.
Myofibroblasts contain smooth muscle actin and pull on the collagen around them, shortening the cord and flexing the finger.
questions.why: Dupuytren contracture is a fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar aponeurosis. Myofibroblasts, which contain alpha smooth muscle actin, multiply in nodules and cords. Their actin and myosin contract and pull on the surrounding collagen, while new collagen stabilizes the shortened tissue. This gradually draws the ring and little fingers into flexion at the MCP and PIP joints. It is more common in older men and in people with diabetes or heavy alcohol use.
whyNot: Correct.
Reflex muscle contraction would relax under anesthesia and would not form a palpable cord in the palm. Spasticity also affects many muscles, not one finger.
Ankylosis after inflammatory arthritis fixes the joint surfaces themselves. His joint is normal, and the limiting structure is a cord in the palm.
The flexor tendons glide normally, which rules out a tethering tendon sheath, as in stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger).

case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen in the evening, and fatigue of her jaw while chewing. Physical examination shows bilateral ptosis that worsens after 60 seconds of sustained upward gaze. Neck flexion and shoulder abduction weaken with repeated effort. Deep tendon reflexes and sensation are normal. Serum antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor are elevated. CT of the chest shows a 4-cm anterior mediastinal mass, and resection shows a thymoma. Diagnosis: generalized myasthenia gravis associated with thymoma.

questions.stem: She is treated with pyridostigmine, and her strength improves. Which of the following best explains this improvement?
options: Longer acetylcholine action at the remaining receptors
More calcium entry through presynaptic channels
Increased SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion in the terminal
Faster synthesis of new nicotinic receptors
approach: Identify the drug class: pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase.
Recall the defect in myasthenia gravis: fewer postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, so the end plate potential is small.
Blocking breakdown keeps acetylcholine in the cleft longer, so it binds the remaining receptors more times and enlarges the end plate potential.
questions.why: At the neuromuscular junction, an action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium triggers SNARE-mediated release of acetylcholine, and acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors to produce an end plate potential. Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal. In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of receptors, so the end plate potential may fail to reach threshold. Pyridostigmine blocks acetylcholinesterase, so each released quantum acts longer and on more receptors, restoring transmission.
whyNot: Correct.
Increasing presynaptic calcium entry is how potassium channel blockers such as 3,4-diaminopyridine help Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Pyridostigmine does not act on the terminal.
Vesicle fusion depends on SNARE proteins and calcium entry. Pyridostigmine acts in the synaptic cleft, not on the release machinery.
Cholinesterase inhibitors do not increase receptor synthesis. Receptor numbers recover only when the antibody attack is reduced, for example by immunotherapy or thymectomy.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the weakness that worsens with repeated effort in this patient?
options: IgG against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Toxin cleavage of SNARE proteins in the nerve terminal
IgG against end plate receptors, with complement injury
CD8+ T cells invading and killing muscle fibers
approach: Note the pattern: fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and limb weakness that worsens with use, plus thymoma.
Recall that myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic disorder caused by antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor.
With repeated firing, release per impulse normally falls a little; with fewer receptors, the end plate potential drops below threshold and fibers drop out.
questions.why: In myasthenia gravis, IgG against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor blocks the receptor, cross-links it so it is internalized faster, and activates complement that damages the postsynaptic folds. The end plate has less safety margin. With repeated stimulation, acetylcholine release per impulse falls normally, and more fibers fail to fire, so weakness worsens with use. Thymic abnormalities (hyperplasia or thymoma) are common. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is the presynaptic opposite: strength improves with brief effort.
whyNot: Antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome, in which strength improves briefly with repeated effort and is linked to small cell lung cancer.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release, causing descending flaccid paralysis with dilated pupils.
Correct.
Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells invading muscle fibers cause polymyositis and inclusion body myositis, which produce weakness that does not fluctuate with use.

questions.stem: Six months later, she develops nasal speech and nasal regurgitation of liquids from fatigable weakness of the muscles of the soft palate and pharynx. These muscles develop from which of the following pharyngeal arches, and which cranial nerve supplies them?
options: Third arch, glossopharyngeal nerve
Fourth arch, vagus nerve
Second arch, facial nerve
First arch, mandibular nerve
approach: Identify the weak muscles: levator veli palatini and the pharyngeal constrictors close off the nasopharynx during speech and swallowing.
Recall the arch origin: most palatal and pharyngeal muscles come from the fourth arch.
Fourth arch muscles are supplied by the vagus nerve through the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.why: Each pharyngeal arch brings its own muscles and cranial nerve. The first arch gives the muscles of mastication (CN V3), the second the muscles of facial expression (CN VII), the third the stylopharyngeus (CN IX), and the fourth and sixth the muscles of the pharynx, soft palate, and larynx (CN X). When myasthenia weakens the levator veli palatini and pharyngeal constrictors, the soft palate cannot seal the nasopharynx. Speech becomes nasal and liquids escape through the nose.
whyNot: The third arch forms only one muscle, the stylopharyngeus, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. It elevates the pharynx but does not close the nasopharynx.
Correct.
The second arch forms the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric, all supplied by the facial nerve.

The first arch forms the muscles of mastication, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani, supplied by CN V3. Her jaw fatigue involves these, but the palatal elevator and constrictors are not first arch muscles.

questions.stem: Before antibody results were available, a single lesion affecting all the cranial nerves that supply her extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris was considered. At which of the following openings do all of these nerves pass together?
options: Optic canal
Foramen rotundum
Inferior orbital fissure
Superior orbital fissure
approach: Name the nerves: oculomotor (levator palpebrae and most extraocular muscles), trochlear (superior oblique), and abducens (lateral rectus).
Recall where they enter the orbit together.
All three, plus the ophthalmic division of CN V, pass through the superior orbital fissure.
questions.why: The oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves run through the cavernous sinus and enter the orbit together through the superior orbital fissure, along with branches of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) and the superior ophthalmic vein. A lesion at the fissure can cause ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and forehead numbness. Her normal sensation, fatigable weakness, and positive antibodies point instead to the neuromuscular junction.
whyNot: The optic canal carries the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery. A lesion there causes visual loss, not ptosis or ophthalmoplegia.
The foramen rotundum carries the maxillary nerve (CN V2), which is sensory to the midface and supplies no eye muscles.
The inferior orbital fissure carries the infraorbital and zygomatic branches of CN V2 and orbital veins, not the motor nerves of the eye.
Correct.

case: A 19-year-old man undergoes general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine for repair of a fractured mandible. Twenty minutes after induction, end-tidal carbon dioxide rises from 38 to 74 mm Hg (35 to 45) despite increased ventilation, and generalized muscle rigidity develops. Temperature rises to 40.6 °C (105.1 °F), pulse is 148/min, and blood pressure is 96/54 mm Hg. Arterial pH is 7.12 (7.35 to 7.45). Serum potassium is 6.6 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). His maternal uncle died during surgery. Genetic testing later shows a heterozygous mutation in RYR1. Diagnosis: malignant hyperthermia.

questions.stem: Intravenous dantrolene is given, and his rigidity and hypercarbia resolve. Which of the following is the site of action of this drug?
options: Dihydropyridine receptor in the T-tubule membrane
Ryanodine receptor in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Calcium ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Nicotinic receptor at the motor end plate
approach: Identify the defect: a mutant RyR1 opens too easily when exposed to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine.
Trace excitation-contraction coupling: T-tubule depolarization, DHPR shape change, RyR1 opening, calcium release, troponin C binding, SERCA reuptake.
The drug that stops the crisis must block the leaking channel, RyR1.
questions.why: In skeletal muscle, depolarization of the T-tubule changes the shape of the dihydropyridine receptor, which is mechanically linked to RyR1 in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. RyR1 opens and releases calcium, which binds troponin C to allow contraction. SERCA then pumps calcium back. In malignant hyperthermia, a mutant RyR1 releases calcium uncontrollably when triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. Dantrolene binds RyR1 and reduces calcium release, ending the rigidity and hypermetabolism.
whyNot: The dihydropyridine receptor is the voltage sensor that triggers release. The defect lies downstream at the release channel, and dantrolene does not block this receptor.
Correct.
SERCA pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to end contraction. Blocking it would raise cytosolic calcium and worsen the crisis.
Blocking nicotinic receptors with a nondepolarizing agent does not stop the crisis, because the calcium leak comes from inside the fiber.

questions.stem: Sustained high cytosolic calcium in his muscle fibers drives continuous cross-bridge cycling, which generates heat and carbon dioxide. Calcium binding to troponin C most directly permits which of the following steps of the cycle?
options: Binding of the cocked myosin head to actin
Hydrolysis of ATP by the free myosin head
Detachment of myosin from actin after ATP binds
Release of ADP at the end of the power stroke
approach: Recall the regulation: at rest, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Calcium binds troponin C, which shifts tropomyosin away from those sites.
The step that needs exposed sites is attachment of the cocked myosin head to actin.
questions.why: The cross-bridge cycle runs in this order: ATP binds myosin and releases it from actin; ATP hydrolysis cocks the head; the head binds actin; phosphate release drives the power stroke; ADP is released, leaving a rigor state until new ATP binds. Calcium binding to troponin C moves tropomyosin and uncovers the binding sites on actin, so the attachment step can occur. In malignant hyperthermia, calcium stays high, cycling and SERCA pumping consume ATP nonstop, and the fibers make heat, carbon dioxide, and lactate.
whyNot: Correct.
Myosin hydrolyzes ATP and cocks its head while detached from actin, and this does not require calcium.
Detachment follows ATP binding to the myosin head and does not depend on troponin. Without ATP, heads stay bound, as in rigor mortis.
ADP release completes the power stroke after the head has bound actin. Calcium acts earlier, at binding.

questions.stem: On the second hospital day, his urine is dark brown. Which of the following urinalysis findings is most likely?
options: Dipstick negative for blood with many RBCs/hpf
Dysmorphic RBCs and red blood cell casts
Dipstick positive for bilirubin, negative for blood
Dipstick positive for blood with 0 to 2 RBCs/hpf
approach: Link the crisis to muscle breakdown: sustained contraction and heat injure fibers (rhabdomyolysis).
Myoglobin released from fibers is filtered by the glomeruli and darkens the urine.
The dipstick heme test reacts with myoglobin, but no red cells are seen on microscopy (normal is 0 to 2 RBCs/hpf).
questions.why: Rhabdomyolysis releases potassium, phosphate, creatine kinase, and myoglobin from injured muscle. Myoglobin is small enough to be filtered and turns the urine red-brown. The dipstick detects the peroxidase activity of the heme group, so it reads positive for blood, yet microscopy shows few or no red cells. Creatine kinase is often above 5 times the upper limit, and hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury from heme pigment toxicity and tubular casts are the main dangers.
whyNot: Many red cells with a negative dipstick is a mismatch that does not fit any common cause of dark urine. Intact red cells in the urine normally make the dipstick positive.
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts indicate glomerular bleeding, as in glomerulonephritis.
Dark urine with bilirubin points to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from liver or biliary disease. Myoglobin gives a positive blood reaction.
Correct.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of his skeletal muscle shows each T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum at the junction of the A and I bands. Which of the following best describes the corresponding structure in normal cardiac muscle?
options: Triads at the A-I junction, identical to skeletal muscle
Caveolae beneath the sarcolemma, with no T-tubules
Dyads, one T-tubule with one cisterna, at the Z line
Triads at the Z line coupled by gap junctions
approach: Identify the structure in the stem: a triad, typical of skeletal muscle.
Recall that cardiac muscle has large T-tubules at the Z lines, each paired with one terminal cisterna (a dyad).
Connect structure to function: cardiac release depends on calcium entry through L-type channels rather than a direct mechanical link.
questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated cells with peripheral nuclei, and each T-tubule sits between two terminal cisternae at the A-I junction, forming a triad. Cardiac muscle cells are branched, have one or two central nuclei, and join at intercalated discs that contain gap junctions and desmosomes. Their T-tubules lie at the Z lines and pair with a single cisterna as a dyad. Smooth muscle cells are fusiform, have a central nucleus, use dense bodies, and lack striations and T-tubules.
whyNot: Triads at the A-I junction are the skeletal arrangement described in the stem. Cardiac muscle has wider T-tubules at the Z lines and less sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Caveolae with no T-tubules and sparse sarcoplasmic reticulum describe smooth muscle, which also lacks striations.
Correct.
Gap junctions couple neighboring cardiac cells at intercalated discs. They do not link T-tubules to sarcoplasmic reticulum, and cardiac couplings are dyads.

topics: Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle histology

dx: Becker muscular dystrophy with dilated cardiomyopathy
case: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of shortness of breath with exertion and swelling of his ankles. He began having calf cramps with exercise at age 12 and over the past few years has had increasing difficulty climbing stairs, but he walks without assistance. His maternal uncle used a wheelchair from age 40 and died of heart failure. Physical examination shows enlarged calves, mild proximal leg weakness, an S3 gallop, and bilateral pitting ankle edema. Serum creatine kinase is 3,800 U/L (30 to 170). Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25% (55 to 70). Muscle biopsy shows reduced dystrophin. Diagnosis: Becker muscular dystrophy with dilated cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of this patient's illness most strongly favors his diagnosis over Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: Enlarged calves with proximal leg weakness
Creatine kinase more than 20 times the upper reference limit
Absence of sensory loss on examination
Symptom onset at age 12, still walking at 24
approach: List what Duchenne and Becker share: X-linked inheritance, calf pseudohypertrophy, proximal weakness, high CK, and cardiomyopathy.
Find the feature that differs: age of onset and rate of progression.
Duchenne begins by about age 5 with loss of walking by about 12; Becker starts later and many still walk into adulthood.
questions.why: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are both X-linked dystrophinopathies. In Duchenne, dystrophin is essentially absent, weakness begins in early childhood, and boys lose the ability to walk by about age 12. In Becker, a truncated, partly functional dystrophin is made, so onset is later, progression is slower, and patients often walk past age 16. Dilated cardiomyopathy can dominate in Becker. Dystrophin immunostaining (absent versus reduced or patchy) and genetic testing separate the two.
whyNot: Calf pseudohypertrophy and proximal weakness occur in both disorders, because both involve dystrophin deficiency.
Very high creatine kinase is found in both Duchenne and Becker disease, so it does not separate them.
Sensation is normal in both, since both are primary muscle diseases.
Correct.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows deletion of three consecutive exons of the DMD gene that together contain 357 nucleotides. Which of the following best explains why his disease is milder than Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: The deletion creates a premature stop codon
Somatic mosaicism limits the mutation to some fibers
The downstream reading frame is preserved
Random X inactivation silences the mutant allele
approach: Check the deletion size: 357 is divisible by 3 (119 codons).
An in-frame deletion removes amino acids but keeps all later codons in the right frame.
The protein is shorter but keeps its end domains, so it partly works, giving the Becker phenotype.
questions.why: The reading frame rule explains most dystrophinopathies. If a deletion removes a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of 3, the frame shifts, a premature stop codon appears, and no functional dystrophin is made (Duchenne). If the deletion is a multiple of 3, the frame is kept, and a shorter protein that still links actin to the sarcolemma is produced (Becker). The DMD gene is one of the largest human genes, more than 2 million base pairs, so it has a high rate of new mutations.
whyNot: A premature stop codon from a frameshift or nonsense mutation abolishes dystrophin, which causes Duchenne disease.
Somatic mosaicism would leave some normal fibers, but this deletion was inherited through his mother's family and is present in all his cells.
Correct.
X inactivation happens only in females. A male has one X chromosome, so his only DMD allele carries the deletion.

questions.stem: He is admitted and treated with dobutamine, a beta-1 adrenergic agonist, and his cardiac output increases. Which of the following best explains the increase in contractility?
options: Phospholamban phosphorylation increases SERCA uptake
Phospholamban dephosphorylation activates SERCA
Depolarization opens RyR2 by direct mechanical coupling
Inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase raises intracellular sodium
approach: Follow the signal: beta-1 receptor, Gs, cAMP, protein kinase A.
PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, which then stops inhibiting SERCA2.
Faster uptake loads the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so each beat releases more calcium through RyR2 and the heart also relaxes faster.
questions.why: In cardiac muscle, calcium entering through L-type channels during the plateau triggers calcium release from RyR2 (calcium-induced calcium release). Beta-1 stimulation raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A. PKA phosphorylates L-type channels, increasing calcium entry, and phospholamban, which releases its brake on SERCA2. The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores more calcium, so later beats are stronger, and relaxation is faster. The long cardiac refractory period prevents these stronger beats from summing into tetany.
whyNot: Correct.
Dephosphorylated phospholamban inhibits SERCA. Beta-1 stimulation phosphorylates it, which removes that inhibition.
Direct mechanical coupling of the voltage sensor to the release channel occurs in skeletal muscle (DHPR to RyR1). Cardiac RyR2 opens in response to calcium entering through L-type channels.
Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is the mechanism of digoxin. It raises sodium, which slows calcium removal by the sodium-calcium exchanger.

questions.stem: Dystrophin anchors the contractile apparatus to the sarcolemma at costameres aligned with the Z lines. On electron microscopy of a contracting fiber, which of the following regions, located in the center of the A band and containing only thick filaments, becomes narrower?
options: I band
H zone
M line
Z line
approach: Locate the region: central part of the A band with thick filaments only.
That region is the H zone.
As thin filaments slide toward the center, they overlap more of the thick filaments, so the H zone narrows.
questions.why: A sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next. The A band is the full length of the thick filaments and stays constant. The I band holds only thin filaments and is split by the Z line. The H zone is the middle of the A band where thick filaments do not overlap thin ones, and the M line runs through its center. During contraction, filaments slide past each other, so the I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length.
whyNot: The I band also narrows during contraction, but it contains only thin filaments and is bisected by the Z line.
Correct.
The M line is the thin central line where thick filaments are cross-linked. Its width does not change.
The Z line anchors the thin filaments at each end of the sarcomere. Z lines move closer together but do not narrow.

case: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of slowly progressive difficulty gripping tools, climbing stairs, and rising from a low chair. He has fallen twice when his knees buckled. Physical examination shows asymmetric weakness and atrophy of the quadriceps and forearm flexor muscles, with weak flexion of the distal interphalangeal joints of all fingers. There is no rash. Sensation and reflexes are normal. Serum creatine kinase is 850 U/L (30 to 170). Muscle biopsy shows endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, and cytoplasmic protein inclusions. A 6-month trial of prednisone did not improve his strength. Diagnosis: inclusion body myositis.

questions.stem: The endomysial infiltrate surrounds and invades fibers that are not necrotic, and the fibers show increased MHC class I expression. Which of the following immune mechanisms does this pattern share with polymyositis?
options: CD8+ T-cell killing of fibers expressing MHC I
Complement membrane attack complex on capillaries
Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors
Immune complex deposition in arteriole walls
approach: Note the pattern: lymphocytes in the endomysium invading non-necrotic fibers, with MHC class I upregulated on the fibers.
MHC class I presents peptides to CD8+ T cells.
This is the cytotoxic T-cell mechanism of polymyositis and inclusion body myositis, which differs from the humoral, capillary-centered injury of dermatomyositis.
questions.why: In polymyositis and inclusion body myositis, muscle fibers express MHC class I, and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells surround and invade them in the endomysium, killing them with perforin and granzymes. In dermatomyositis, antibodies and complement attack endomysial capillaries, leading to capillary loss, perivascular inflammation in the perimysium, and perifascicular atrophy. Dermatomyositis adds a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules and has a link to internal cancer. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies in either may signal interstitial lung disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Complement attack on endomysial capillaries is the mechanism of dermatomyositis. It produces perimysial inflammation and perifascicular atrophy, not T cells invading single fibers.
Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, with fatigable weakness and normal muscle biopsy.
Immune complex deposition in vessels causes vasculitis, as in polyarteritis nodosa, with transmural vessel inflammation and infarcts.

questions.stem: His prednisone had been continued for 6 months while his strength declined further. At that time, serum creatine kinase was 790 U/L (30 to 170). Which of the following findings most strongly favored ongoing myositis over glucocorticoid-induced myopathy as the cause of the decline?
options: Proximal leg weakness on examination
Atrophy of type II fibers without inflammation on biopsy
Rounded face and abdominal striae
Persistently elevated serum creatine kinase
approach: Recall what each disorder does to fibers: myositis kills fibers, and steroid myopathy shrinks type II fibers without killing them.
Fiber necrosis releases creatine kinase into the blood.
A CK that stays high on treatment points to active myositis; steroid myopathy has a normal CK.
questions.why: Inflammatory myositis destroys muscle fibers, so creatine kinase is high and the biopsy shows inflammation and necrosis. Glucocorticoid myopathy causes atrophy of type II fibers without necrosis, so creatine kinase is normal. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal pain and stiffness with normal strength and normal creatine kinase. When weakness worsens during steroid treatment, a persistently high creatine kinase favors active myositis, as seen in inclusion body myositis, which typically does not respond to steroids.
whyNot: Proximal leg weakness occurs in both myositis and steroid myopathy, so it does not separate them.
Type II fiber atrophy without inflammation is the biopsy finding of steroid myopathy, the opposite of what favors myositis.
Cushingoid features show glucocorticoid exposure but say nothing about which disorder is causing the weakness.
Correct.

topics: Myositis versus steroid myopathy and polymyalgia rheumatica

questions.stem: Gomori trichrome staining of the biopsy also shows scattered ragged red fibers, and some fibers lack cytochrome c oxidase activity. Which of the following best explains the ragged red appearance of these fibers?
options: Glycogen accumulated in vacuoles of the sarcoplasm
Subsarcolemmal clumps of abnormal mitochondria
Rod-shaped Z-disc material in the fibers
Lymphocytes clustered beneath the sarcolemma
approach: Recall that the Gomori trichrome stain colors mitochondria red.
When defective mitochondria multiply as compensation, they collect under the sarcolemma and give the fiber a ragged red border.
Loss of cytochrome c oxidase activity confirms a respiratory chain defect in those fibers.
questions.why: Ragged red fibers are fibers with clumps of proliferated, abnormal mitochondria under the sarcolemma, seen with Gomori trichrome. They mark mitochondrial dysfunction. In primary mitochondrial myopathies such as MERRF and MELAS, mutant mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother, and the mix of normal and mutant genomes (heteroplasmy) varies among tissues and relatives, so severity varies. Inclusion body myositis shows more ragged red and cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibers than expected for age, from acquired mitochondrial DNA deletions.
whyNot: Glycogen-filled vacuoles are seen in glycogen storage myopathies such as Pompe disease and stain with PAS, not as red rims on trichrome.
Correct.
Rod-shaped Z-disc material (nemaline rods) characterizes nemaline myopathy, a congenital myopathy.
Lymphocytes lie between fibers in the endomysium. They do not form the red, irregular rim inside single fibers.

questions.stem: Weak flexion at the distal interphalangeal joints of all four fingers was first thought to reflect a single peripheral nerve lesion. Which of the following facts makes a single nerve lesion unlikely?
options: The radial nerve alone supplies the long finger flexors
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the deep flexors
The median and ulnar nerves share supply of the muscle
The ulnar nerve alone supplies all deep finger flexors
approach: Name the muscle: flexor digitorum profundus flexes the distal interphalangeal joints.
Recall its split supply: the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve to the index and middle fingers, and the ulnar nerve to the ring and little fingers.
Weakness in all four fingers would need lesions of two nerves, so a muscle disorder is more likely.
questions.why: Flexor digitorum profundus has a dual nerve supply. The median nerve, through its anterior interosseous branch, supplies the slips to the index and middle fingers, and the ulnar nerve supplies the slips to the ring and little fingers. A median nerve lesion weakens the first two and also impairs thumb opposition. An ulnar lesion at or above the elbow weakens the last two and the small muscles of the hand. Symmetric weakness of all four slips, with normal sensation, points to a muscle disease such as inclusion body myositis.
whyNot: The radial nerve supplies the extensors of the wrist and fingers. A radial lesion causes wrist drop, not weak finger flexion.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm muscles (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) and weakens elbow flexion, not the fingers.
Correct.
The ulnar nerve supplies only the part of flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers. An ulnar lesion at the elbow weakens distal flexion of only those two fingers.

dx: Giant cell tumor of the distal femoral epiphysis
case: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of aching pain and swelling above her left knee. Physical examination shows a tender, firm swelling of the distal lateral thigh and mildly limited knee flexion. Radiographs show an eccentric lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal femur that extends to the subchondral bone, with an expanded, thin cortical rim and a soap-bubble appearance. There is no matrix mineralization or periosteal reaction. Serum calcium and alkaline phosphatase are within the reference ranges. Biopsy shows sheets of mononuclear stromal cells with many evenly scattered osteoclast-like giant cells. Diagnosis: giant cell tumor of bone.

questions.stem: Her 35-year-old sister has a slowly growing, firm nodule on the palmar side of her index finger attached to a flexor tendon sheath. Excision shows mononuclear cells, multinucleated giant cells, foamy macrophages, and hemosiderin. Overexpression of which of the following by the neoplastic cells recruits most of the cells in the sister's lesion?
options: Receptor activator of NF-kB ligand
Parathyroid hormone-related protein
Colony-stimulating factor 1
Fibroblast growth factor 23
approach: Recognize the sister's lesion: a giant cell tumor of tendon sheath (tenosynovial giant cell tumor).
Recall that only a small fraction of its cells are neoplastic, and they overexpress CSF1, often from a translocation.
CSF1 attracts macrophages and giant cells bearing its receptor, which make up most of the mass.
questions.why: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor arises from the synovium of joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, most often in the fingers or knee. A minority of neoplastic cells overexpress colony-stimulating factor 1, frequently because of a translocation involving CSF1. CSF1 recruits macrophages, giant cells, and foamy cells that form most of the tumor (a landscape effect). Giant cell tumor of bone is different: neoplastic stromal cells with H3F3A mutations express RANKL and drive osteoclast-like giant cells, producing an epiphyseal soap-bubble lesion in young adults.
whyNot: RANKL made by neoplastic stromal cells drives the osteoclast-like giant cells of giant cell tumor of bone, the patient's own tumor. It is not the driver of the tendon sheath tumor.
PTHrP is secreted by some carcinomas, such as squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, and causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.
Correct.
FGF23 is made by phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors and causes tumor-induced osteomalacia with low phosphate.

questions.stem: The giant cells in her tumor resorb bone by pumping protons into a sealed space beneath the ruffled border. In a child with autosomal recessive osteopetrosis from a CLCN7 mutation, which of the following steps of this process fails?
options: Chloride movement that balances proton secretion
Carbonic anhydrase production of protons
RANKL-driven fusion of mononuclear osteoclast precursors
Cathepsin K digestion of type I collagen
approach: Trace resorption: carbonic anhydrase II makes protons, a proton pump moves them into the resorption pit, and chloride follows through the CLC-7 channel.
Without chloride flow, charge builds up and the pump stops, so the pit cannot be acidified.
Mineral is not dissolved, so bone builds up but is brittle.
questions.why: Osteoclasts seal onto bone and secrete hydrochloric acid through the ruffled border. Carbonic anhydrase II produces protons, a vacuolar proton ATPase pumps them out, and chloride follows through the CLC-7 chloride channel to keep charge balanced. A CLCN7 mutation stops this acidification, so osteoclasts cannot dissolve bone mineral. The bone becomes dense but brittle, and marrow space shrinks, causing anemia, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and cranial nerve compression in severe forms.
whyNot: Correct.
Carbonic anhydrase II supplies the protons. Its deficiency causes a different form of osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification.
Defects in RANKL or its receptor RANK give osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis. CLCN7 mutations leave osteoclasts present but unable to resorb.
Cathepsin K deficiency causes pycnodysostosis, in which acid dissolves mineral but the collagen matrix is not digested.

questions.stem: Her radiologist also reviews images from a 22-year-old man who has multiple intramedullary cartilage lesions in the bones of both hands and several soft tissue hemangiomas. Which of the following best describes his condition and its main long-term risk?
options: Ollier disease, with risk of osteosarcoma
Maffucci syndrome, with risk of chondrosarcoma
Multiple hereditary exostoses, with risk of Ewing sarcoma
Maffucci syndrome, with risk of giant cell tumor
approach: Identify the lesion: intramedullary hyaline cartilage in hand bones is an enchondroma.
Multiple enchondromas alone are Ollier disease; with soft tissue hemangiomas, Maffucci syndrome.
Both carry a high risk of transformation of an enchondroma to chondrosarcoma.
questions.why: An enchondroma is a benign nodule of hyaline cartilage inside the medullary cavity, most often in the small bones of the hands. Multiple enchondromas are Ollier disease, and multiple enchondromas with soft tissue hemangiomas are Maffucci syndrome. Both carry a substantial risk of chondrosarcoma, and Maffucci syndrome also raises the risk of other cancers. Osteochondroma, by contrast, is a bony stalk on the metaphyseal surface, continuous with the marrow and capped by cartilage, and is multiple in EXT1 or EXT2 hereditary exostoses.
whyNot: Ollier disease is multiple enchondromas without hemangiomas. Its main risk is chondrosarcoma, not osteosarcoma.
Correct.
Multiple hereditary exostoses (EXT1 or EXT2) produce metaphyseal bony stalks capped by cartilage on the surface of bone, not lesions inside the marrow. Their risk is chondrosarcoma.
Maffucci syndrome is the right diagnosis, but its main malignant risk is chondrosarcoma. It is not linked to giant cell tumor.

topics: Enchondroma, Ollier disease, and Maffucci syndrome

questions.stem: Before biopsy, the differential diagnosis for her painful bone lesion included osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma. Which of the following findings would favor osteoblastoma over osteoid osteoma in a patient with a bone-forming tumor?
options: A cortical nidus under 1.5 cm surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis
Night pain promptly relieved by aspirin
Onset in an adolescent male
A 4-cm lesion in the posterior elements of a vertebra
approach: Recall that osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma have similar histology: woven bone trabeculae rimmed by osteoblasts.
They are separated by size, site, and pain pattern.
Osteoblastoma is larger than 2 cm, favors the posterior elements of the spine, and causes dull pain not relieved by NSAIDs.
questions.why: Osteoid osteoma is a small (under 2 cm) cortical nidus with a sclerotic rim, often in the femur or tibia of young males. The nidus produces prostaglandin E2 through cyclooxygenase, which causes night pain that NSAIDs relieve well. Osteoblastoma has the same histology but is larger than 2 cm, often arises in the posterior elements of the vertebrae, has less reactive sclerosis, and causes dull pain that responds poorly to NSAIDs.
whyNot: A small cortical nidus with dense surrounding sclerosis is the classic radiograph of osteoid osteoma.
Night pain relieved by aspirin or other NSAIDs is typical of osteoid osteoma, whose nidus makes prostaglandin E2. Osteoblastoma pain responds poorly.
Both tumors occur mostly in adolescents and young adults, with a male predominance, so this does not separate them.
Correct.

dx: Osteoblastic metastatic prostate cancer to the lumbar spine
case: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of low back pain that is worse at night. He has had urinary frequency and a weak urinary stream for 2 years. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, nodular prostate. Serum prostate-specific antigen is 86 ng/mL (less than 4). Serum alkaline phosphatase is 410 U/L (40 to 120), and serum calcium is 9.0 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). Radiographs show multiple dense, sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebral bodies and pelvis. Biopsy of an iliac lesion shows prostatic adenocarcinoma surrounded by reactive new bone. Diagnosis: osteoblastic metastatic prostate cancer.

questions.stem: His 64-year-old brother has clear cell renal cell carcinoma with a metastasis to the proximal femur. Compared with this patient's lesions, the brother's bone lesion is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Dense sclerosis with a high alkaline phosphatase
Lytic bone destruction with a risk of hypercalcemia
Mixed lytic and sclerotic areas with hypocalcemia
Periosteal onion-skin layering with a soft tissue mass
approach: Recall the patterns: prostate is osteoblastic; kidney, thyroid, and lung are osteolytic; breast is often mixed.
Lytic metastases make tumor and stromal cells drive osteoclasts to destroy bone.
Bone destruction releases calcium and weakens bone, so hypercalcemia and pathologic fracture follow.
questions.why: Metastases are the most common malignant tumors in bone because many common carcinomas spread through the blood to the red marrow of the axial skeleton and proximal long bones. Renal, thyroid, and lung cancers usually produce lytic lesions by stimulating osteoclasts, often through PTHrP and RANKL. These lesions can cause hypercalcemia and pathologic fractures. Prostate cancer stimulates osteoblasts and produces sclerotic lesions with high alkaline phosphatase, while breast cancer often gives mixed lesions.
whyNot: Dense sclerosis with high alkaline phosphatase is the osteoblastic pattern of prostate cancer, seen in this patient.
Correct.
Mixed lesions are typical of breast cancer, and hypocalcemia is not their expected complication.
Onion-skin periosteal layering is a feature of Ewing sarcoma, a primary tumor of children and adolescents.

questions.stem: A sclerotic lesion is also seen in a vertebra whose transverse processes each contain a foramen. Which of the following best describes this vertebra's region and the function of these foramina?
options: Thoracic; they receive the heads of the ribs
Lumbar; they transmit the lumbar spinal nerves
Cervical; they transmit the vertebral arteries
Sacral; they transmit the sacral nerve rami
approach: Identify the feature: a foramen in each transverse process (foramen transversarium).
This feature is found only in cervical vertebrae.
In C1 to C6 these foramina carry the vertebral arteries up to the skull.
questions.why: Each region of the spine has distinct features that fit its job. Cervical vertebrae have small bodies, bifid spines from C3 to C6, and transverse foramina that carry the vertebral arteries. The atlas has no body and the axis has the dens, which allows head rotation. Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for the ribs. Lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies because they carry the most body weight.
whyNot: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets on the bodies and transverse processes for the ribs, not foramina in the transverse processes.
Lumbar vertebrae have large, kidney-shaped bodies and no transverse foramina. Lumbar spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina between vertebrae.
Correct.
The sacrum has anterior and posterior sacral foramina for the rami of sacral nerves, but it has no separate transverse processes with foramina.

questions.stem: He begins androgen deprivation therapy. Two years later, dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry of the hip shows a T-score of minus 1.8. He has had no fractures. Which of the following best classifies his bone density?
options: Normal bone density
Osteoporosis
Severe osteoporosis
Osteopenia
approach: Recall what the T-score compares: the patient's density with that of a healthy young adult, in standard deviations.
Apply the cutoffs: minus 1.0 or higher is normal; between minus 1.0 and minus 2.5 is osteopenia; minus 2.5 or lower is osteoporosis.
Minus 1.8 falls in the osteopenia range.
questions.why: Androgen deprivation lowers testosterone and the estradiol made from it, and estrogen loss increases RANKL-driven bone resorption. DEXA reports a T-score, the number of standard deviations from the young adult mean. A T-score of minus 1.0 or higher is normal, between minus 1.0 and minus 2.5 is osteopenia, and minus 2.5 or lower is osteoporosis. Osteoporosis leaves serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase normal and presents with vertebral compression, hip, and distal radius fractures, height loss, and kyphosis.
whyNot: Normal bone density is a T-score of minus 1.0 or higher.
Osteoporosis requires a T-score of minus 2.5 or lower, or a fragility fracture of the hip or spine.
Severe (established) osteoporosis is a T-score of minus 2.5 or lower together with one or more fragility fractures.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before biopsy, Paget disease of bone was considered because of his high alkaline phosphatase and sclerotic vertebrae. Which of the following sequences of bone cell activity characterizes Paget disease?
options: Osteoclast resorption, then disorganized new bone
Osteoblast formation, then osteoclast removal of excess
Failed osteoclast resorption with retained cartilage
Normal remodeling with failure of osteoid mineralization
approach: Recall the three phases of Paget disease: lytic, mixed, and sclerotic.
Large, overactive osteoclasts resorb bone first.
Osteoblasts then lay down new bone quickly and chaotically, raising alkaline phosphatase and creating thick but weak mosaic bone.
questions.why: Paget disease starts with abnormally large osteoclasts with many nuclei that resorb bone excessively (lytic phase). Osteoblasts respond with rapid, disorganized bone formation (mixed phase), and finally dense, sclerotic bone remains (burnt-out phase). The new bone is a mosaic of lamellar bone with irregular cement lines, thick but mechanically weak. High osteoblast activity raises alkaline phosphatase, while calcium and phosphate usually stay normal.
whyNot: Correct.
Bone formation does not start the process in Paget disease. Abnormal, overactive osteoclasts begin each lesion.
Failed osteoclast resorption with retained cartilage cores is osteopetrosis, which gives dense bone and normal alkaline phosphatase.
Unmineralized osteoid with normal remodeling describes osteomalacia, which shows low calcium or phosphate and high PTH.

dx: Rotator cuff tear after anterior shoulder dislocation with axillary nerve injury
case: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 hour after falling onto his outstretched right arm while skiing. The arm is held slightly abducted and externally rotated, and the shoulder has lost its rounded contour. Radiographs show an anterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint without fracture. After closed reduction, he has numbness over the lateral upper arm. Three weeks later, deltoid contraction is weak, and he cannot actively raise the arm from his side. MRI shows full-thickness tears of two rotator cuff tendons. Diagnosis: rotator cuff tear after anterior shoulder dislocation, with axillary nerve injury.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of the glenohumeral joint best explains why it depends on the rotator cuff for stability?
options: A deep socket enclosed by a strong labrum
Strong intrinsic ligaments that limit all rotation
A loose capsule reinforced only on its inferior side
A large humeral head on a small, shallow glenoid
approach: Compare bony fit: only a small part of the large humeral head touches the shallow glenoid at any time.
With little bony or ligamentous restraint, stability must come from muscle.
The rotator cuff tendons press the head into the glenoid during movement.
questions.why: The glenohumeral joint gives up stability for range of motion. The humeral head is about three to four times the area of the shallow glenoid, the labrum deepens it only slightly, and the capsule is loose. The supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis compress the head into the glenoid throughout movement. Anterior dislocation stretches the axillary nerve around the surgical neck, causing deltoid weakness and lateral shoulder numbness, and in older adults often tears the cuff.
whyNot: A deep socket describes the hip, where the acetabulum and labrum hold the femoral head securely. The glenoid is shallow even with its labrum.
The glenohumeral ligaments are thin capsular thickenings and allow wide rotation. Strong limiting ligaments would trade mobility for stability.
The capsule is loose, but its weakest part is inferior, which is why the humeral head usually dislocates anteriorly and inferiorly.
Correct.

questions.stem: When his hand is placed behind his lower back, he cannot lift it away from his back. Which of the following muscles and nerves is most likely affected?
options: Teres minor; axillary nerve
Subscapularis; subscapular nerves
Infraspinatus; suprascapular nerve
Latissimus dorsi; thoracodorsal nerve
approach: Identify the movement: lifting the hand off the back requires strong medial rotation with the arm extended (lift-off test).
The rotator cuff muscle that medially rotates the arm is subscapularis.
Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves from the posterior cord.
questions.why: The four rotator cuff muscles each have one main action and nerve. Supraspinatus starts abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve. Infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm (suprascapular nerve), teres minor laterally rotates the arm (axillary nerve), and subscapularis medially rotates the arm (upper and lower subscapular nerves). Supraspinatus is the most often torn. Anterior dislocation in older adults can also tear subscapularis, which shows as a positive lift-off test.
whyNot: Teres minor laterally rotates the arm. Weakness shows as poor external rotation, not failure of this test.
Correct.
Infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm and is tested by resisted external rotation with the elbow at the side.
Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm, but the lift-off test isolates subscapularis, and latissimus is not a rotator cuff muscle.

questions.stem: Persistent loss of shoulder motion after an injury is sometimes caused by adhesive capsulitis. Which of the following examination findings would best support a rotator cuff tear over adhesive capsulitis in this patient?
options: Equal loss of active and passive external rotation
Pain at night when lying on the affected side
Full passive motion with weak active abduction
Tenderness over the anterior joint line
approach: Ask what limits motion: a torn tendon cannot move the arm, but a thickened capsule physically blocks it.
A cuff tear or nerve injury reduces active motion while the examiner can still move the arm through a full range.
Adhesive capsulitis reduces active and passive motion equally.
questions.why: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is inflammation followed by fibrosis and contraction of the glenohumeral capsule. Because the capsule itself is tight, both active and passive motion are lost, with external rotation affected early. It is more common in people with diabetes. In a rotator cuff tear or axillary nerve palsy, the joint is free but the motor is weak, so passive motion is preserved while active motion is lost.
whyNot: Equal loss of active and passive motion, especially external rotation, is the hallmark of adhesive capsulitis, because the stiff capsule blocks movement no matter who moves the arm.
Night pain on lying on the shoulder is common in both cuff tears and adhesive capsulitis, so it does not separate them.
Correct.
Anterior joint line tenderness is nonspecific and occurs with many shoulder problems.

topics: Active versus passive range of motion

questions.stem: Before the fall, he had several months of right shoulder pain during overhead work, which was attributed to subacromial bursitis with impingement. Which of the following findings would have been most typical of that condition?
options: Pain between about 60 and 120 degrees of abduction
Pain only in the final 20 degrees of overhead elevation
Fluctuant swelling over the point of the elbow
Pain with resisted elbow flexion and supination
approach: Locate the bursa: the subacromial bursa lies between the acromion and the supraspinatus tendon.
During abduction, the greater tubercle and tendon pass under the acromion through a middle range of motion.
Compression in that range produces a painful arc of about 60 to 120 degrees.
questions.why: The subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa cushions the supraspinatus tendon under the acromion and coracoacromial ligament. Repeated overhead work narrows this space, and the bursa and tendon are squeezed in the middle of abduction, producing a painful arc from about 60 to 120 degrees. Other common bursitis sites include prepatellar bursitis from kneeling, olecranon bursitis from leaning on the elbow, and trochanteric bursitis from overuse. Septic bursitis is usually from Staphylococcus aureus.
whyNot: Correct.
Pain only at the top of elevation, near 160 to 180 degrees, points to the acromioclavicular joint.
Fluctuant swelling at the point of the elbow is olecranon bursitis, from leaning on the elbow or trauma.
Pain with resisted elbow flexion and supination localizes to the long head of the biceps tendon.
